clinicalPearls: Diphyllobothriasis is caused by broad or fish tapeworms of the genus Diphyllobothrium, acquired by eating raw or undercooked freshwater or anadromous fish containing infective larvae
It occurs where such fish are eaten uncooked, including in dishes like sushi, sashimi, ceviche and marinated raw fish, and the adult is among the longest human tapeworms
Most infections cause few symptoms, but some patients report abdominal discomfort, bloating, diarrhoea or the passage of proglottids
The hallmark complication is vitamin B12 deficiency, because the worm competes for and avidly takes up dietary B12, which can lead to megaloblastic anaemia and, uncommonly, neurological features
Diagnosis is by finding the characteristic operculated eggs, or chains of proglottids, on stool microscopy
A dietary history of raw freshwater or migratory fish consumption is an important clue
Praziquantel is the treatment of choice, with vitamin B12 replacement where deficiency and anaemia have developed
reference.pathophysiology: The adult Diphyllobothrium attaches by its bothria to the small-intestinal mucosa and can reach great length. Humans are infected by eating raw or undercooked fish harbouring the plerocercoid larva, which develops into the adult tapeworm over weeks. Positioned in the proximal small intestine, the worm competes with the host for luminal vitamin B12, binding and absorbing it far more efficiently than the host and thereby depleting available B12; with a favourably situated heavy worm, this can produce B12 deficiency with megaloblastic anaemia and, occasionally, subacute combined degeneration and other neurological manifestations. Local symptoms are otherwise mild and reflect the mechanical presence of the worm rather than tissue invasion.
additionalDifferentials: Other tapeworm infections such as taeniasis and hymenolepiasis
Pernicious anaemia and other causes of vitamin B12 deficiency
Other causes of megaloblastic anaemia including folate deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy for operculated eggs or proglottids
Full blood count and film for macrocytosis and megaloblastic changes
Additional haematinics such as folate to clarify the anaemia
Molecular or morphological identification of the tapeworm species
Dietary and travel history focused on raw fish consumption
redFlags: Symptomatic megaloblastic anaemia with cardiovascular compromise
Neurological features suggesting B12-related subacute combined degeneration
Intestinal obstruction from a very heavy worm burden
reference.prognosis: Excellent; the tapeworm is readily eradicated, and B12 deficiency with its haematological and neurological consequences resolves with treatment and vitamin replacement, though established neurological damage may only partly recover.
pitfalls: Investigating megaloblastic anaemia without considering fish tapeworm in those who eat raw fish
Overlooking the dietary history that points to the diagnosis
Treating the anaemia without eradicating the worm
Assuming all megaloblastic anaemia is due to pernicious anaemia
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Anthelmintic eradication of the tapeworm with a single course of praziquantel, or niclosamide as an alternative
Vitamin B12 replacement to correct deficiency and the resulting megaloblastic anaemia
Confirm cure with follow-up stool examination for eggs or proglottids
Dietary prevention advice to cook or adequately freeze freshwater and anadromous fish and to avoid raw preparations
Monitor recovery of the blood count and any neurological features of B12 deficiency
Public health awareness where locally relevant, given the food-borne source
